claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy contains nonequilibrium chemical short-range order.
Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order can arise from nonequilibrium alloy-processing events.
Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order drives the nucleation of intermetallic precipitates during thermal exposure.
Continued annealing causes growth and eventual coarsening of the nucleated intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloys have a tendency to form intermetallic compounds.
Phase decomposition selectively partitions Mg and other reactive elements into or around the evolving phases.
A fine, uniform dispersion of intermetallics helps maintain a continuous protective oxide film.
A TiO2-rich surface film can enhance passivation and reduce corrosion current in an Mg-Ti-Zn alloy.
A protective MgO or TiO2 film preserves both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation resistance in the proposed alloy.
Excessive intermetallic coarsening fragments or otherwise disrupts the protective oxide film.
Loss of oxide-film continuity increases corrosion rate.
Loss of oxide-film continuity reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Moderate thermal treatment will produce fine, homogeneously distributed intermetallic precipitates.
Moderately annealed samples will retain corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
Excessively annealed samples will show coarsened intermetallics and significantly worse corrosion and oxidation performance than the initial state.
The as-cast metastable solid solution has a relatively homogeneous microstructure and moderate environmental resistance because its alloying elements are well distributed.
Prolonged exposure above approximately 400 °C is sufficient to activate intermetallic precipitation in the proposed alloy.
NaCl solution exposure is an applicable corrosion-test environment for Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloys.
